question: First heart sound (S1) is primarily associated with:
explanation:
• S1 is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid (AV) valves at the start of ventricular systole and is best heard at the apex.
• Closure of the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves produces S2, not S1.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — The Heart Sounds and the Cardiac Cycle

question: Normal stroke volume is approximately:
explanation:
• Stroke volume is the blood ejected by the left ventricle in one beat, normally about 70 mL with a usual range of 60–100 mL.
• With a heart rate of about 70/min this gives the normal cardiac output of roughly 5 L/min.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Cardiac Output, Venous Return and Their Regulation

question: Tidal volume is:
options: B. Normal breath in and out
D. Air left after maximal expiration
explanation:
• Tidal volume is the air moved in or out during one quiet breath, about 500 mL in an adult.
• The extra air taken in on maximal inspiration is the inspiratory reserve volume, and the air remaining after maximal expiration is the residual volume.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Pulmonary Ventilation: Lung Volumes and Capacities

question: Functional residual capacity (FRC) equals:
explanation:
• Functional residual capacity is the air left in the lungs after a normal quiet expiration, so FRC = expiratory reserve volume + residual volume (about 2300 mL).
• TV + IRV is the inspiratory capacity, and VC + RV is total lung capacity.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Pulmonary Ventilation: Lung Volumes and Capacities

question: Cranial nerve III supplies:
options: B. Most extraocular muscles and pupillary constriction
explanation:
• The oculomotor nerve supplies all extraocular muscles except the lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV), plus levator palpebrae superioris and the parasympathetic fibres that constrict the pupil.
• A third nerve palsy therefore gives ptosis, a 'down and out' eye and a fixed dilated pupil.
citation: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy 8e (Head, Neck and Brain) — The Cranial Nerves

question: Facial nerve (CN VII) motor nucleus innervates:
explanation:
• The facial nerve motor nucleus supplies the muscles of facial expression (and stapedius, stylohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric).
• Masseter is supplied by the mandibular division of CN V, superior oblique by CN IV and stylopharyngeus by CN IX.
citation: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy 8e (Head, Neck and Brain) — The Cranial Nerves

question: Insulin is secreted by:
options: B. Beta cells of pancreatic islets
explanation:
• Insulin is secreted by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans, which form about 60% of islet cells.
• Alpha cells secrete glucagon and delta cells secrete somatostatin, so neither can be the source of insulin.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Insulin, Glucagon and Diabetes Mellitus

question: Primary site of tubular reabsorption:
explanation:
• About 65% of the filtered sodium and water, and essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids, are reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, making it the major site of tubular reabsorption.
• The loop of Henle and collecting duct only fine-tune what remains, and Bowman's capsule filters rather than reabsorbs.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Tubular Reabsorption and Secretion by the Kidneys

question: Parietal cells secrete:
explanation:
• Gastric parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, the latter essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.
• Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and surface cells secrete mucus, which is why gastrectomy or atrophic gastritis causes B12 deficiency.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Secretory Functions of the Alimentary Tract

question: O negative blood is considered universal donor for:
explanation:
• O-negative red cells carry neither A/B antigens nor the RhD antigen, so they can be given as emergency uncross-matched packed cells to a recipient of any group.
• For plasma the universal donor is group AB, because AB plasma contains no anti-A or anti-B antibodies.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Blood Types; Transfusion; Tissue Transplantation

question: Cardiac output equals:
explanation:
• Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, normally about 5 L/min in a resting adult.
• EDV – ESV defines stroke volume itself, while MAP = CO × SVR describes arterial pressure rather than output.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Cardiac Output, Venous Return and Their Regulation

question: Main site of gas exchange:
explanation:
• Gas exchange occurs across the thin alveolar–capillary (respiratory) membrane, where the huge surface area allows rapid diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
• The larynx, trachea and bronchi are conducting airways that form anatomical dead space and take no part in exchange.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Physical Principles of Gas Exchange; Diffusion Through the Respiratory Membrane

question: CSF is mainly produced in:
explanation:
• About two-thirds of CSF is secreted by the choroid plexuses of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles, at roughly 500 mL per day.
• It is reabsorbed into venous blood through the arachnoid granulations, so blocked absorption there causes communicating hydrocephalus.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Cerebral Blood Flow, Cerebrospinal Fluid and Brain Metabolism

question: TSH is secreted by:
explanation:
• TSH is a tropic hormone of the anterior pituitary that stimulates the thyroid to release T3 and T4.
• The posterior pituitary stores only ADH and oxytocin, so a raised TSH with a low T4 indicates primary hypothyroidism.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — The Pituitary Hormones and Their Control by the Hypothalamus

question: Ball-and-socket joint example:
explanation:
• The shoulder (glenohumeral) joint, like the hip, is a ball-and-socket synovial joint allowing movement in all three planes plus rotation.
• The elbow and ankle are hinge joints that permit only flexion and extension.
citation: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy 8e (Upper Limb and Thorax) — Joints of the Upper Limb

question: Antibody-mediated immunity is called:
explanation:
• Antibody-mediated immunity is called humoral immunity because it is carried out by B lymphocytes and the plasma cells derived from them, which secrete immunoglobulins into body fluids.
• Cell-mediated immunity is a T-lymphocyte function responsible for graft rejection and defence against intracellular organisms.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Immunity: Humoral and Cell-Mediated Immune Response

question: P wave on ECG represents:
explanation:
• The P wave records atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex ventricular depolarisation and the T wave ventricular repolarisation.
• Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular rhythm therefore suggest atrial fibrillation.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — The Normal Electrocardiogram

question: Hypoxemia with normal A-a gradient suggests:
explanation:
• Hypoventilation lowers alveolar oxygen without impairing transfer across the membrane, so the A–a gradient stays normal while the PaCO2 rises.
• Shunt, V/Q mismatch and diffusion limitation all widen the A–a gradient, so a normal gradient effectively excludes them.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Respiratory Insufficiency: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis and Oxygen Therapy

question: Juxtaglomerular cells release:
explanation:
• Juxtaglomerular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole release renin when renal perfusion pressure, distal sodium delivery or sympathetic tone changes, initiating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone cascade.
• Aldosterone itself comes from the adrenal zona glomerulosa and ADH from the posterior pituitary.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e — Renal Regulation of Blood Pressure: The Renin-Angiotensin System

question: Common bile duct joins pancreatic duct at:
explanation:
• The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct unite at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), which opens on the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum and is guarded by the sphincter of Oddi.
• A stone impacted here can cause both obstructive jaundice and acute pancreatitis.
citation: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy 8e (Abdomen and Lower Limb) — The Extrahepatic Biliary Apparatus

question: Anatomy & Physiology Q21: The thymus is primarily important for:
explanation:
• T lymphocytes mature in the thymus.
• B cells mature in bone marrow.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Immunology: Cells and Organs of the Immune System

question: A staff nurse records a blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg in an adult. The mean arterial pressure (MAP) is approximately:
explanation: MAP is estimated as diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure, because at normal heart rates diastole occupies about two-thirds of the cardiac cycle: 90 + (60/3) = 110 mmHg. The tempting answer is 120 mmHg, which is the plain average of systolic and diastolic pressure; that overestimates MAP because it wrongly assumes the heart spends equal time in systole and diastole.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Arterial Pressure Regulation

question: A patient in sustained supraventricular tachycardia at 190 beats/min develops chest pain. The main reason myocardial perfusion falls at very high heart rates is that:
options: A. Diastole shortens far more than systole, and the left ventricle is perfused mainly during diastole
B. The coronary arteries constrict in response to tachycardia
C. Systole shortens, so less blood enters the coronary ostia
D. Myocardial oxygen extraction falls as the heart rate rises
explanation: Left ventricular subendocardial vessels are compressed during systole, so coronary flow occurs almost entirely in diastole; as rate rises, diastole is the phase that is sacrificed, cutting supply exactly when demand is highest. Option B is wrong because increased cardiac work releases adenosine and other metabolites that cause coronary vasodilatation, not constriction.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Coronary Circulation

question: According to the Frank-Starling law of the heart, an increase in venous return raises stroke volume because:
options: A. It directly increases the heart rate through stretch receptors in the sinoatrial node
B. It lowers systemic vascular resistance
C. It raises the calcium concentration of blood entering the coronary arteries
D. Greater end-diastolic stretch of the myocardial fibres increases their force of contraction
explanation: Stretching cardiac muscle to a more favourable actin-myosin overlap and increasing troponin C calcium sensitivity makes the next contraction more forceful, so the heart pumps out whatever venous return delivers. Option A describes the Bainbridge reflex, which does raise heart rate on atrial stretch, but it changes rate rather than the force of each beat and so does not explain the rise in stroke volume.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Heart Muscle: The Heart as a Pump

question: In arterial blood, oxygen is transported mainly:
options: C. Bound to haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin
explanation: About 98% of oxygen is carried chemically bound to haemoglobin, each gram of which carries roughly 1.34 mL of oxygen when fully saturated. Only about 1.5% travels dissolved in plasma, and although that tiny fraction is what the PaO2 measures, it cannot meet tissue demand, which is why a severely anaemic patient can be tissue-hypoxic despite a normal PaO2. Bicarbonate is a mode of carbon dioxide transport, not oxygen.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide in Blood

question: The peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies increase ventilation mainly in response to:
options: A. A fall in arterial PO2 below about 60 mmHg
B. A rise in arterial PO2 above 100 mmHg
C. A fall in arterial PCO2
D. A rise in plasma bicarbonate
explanation: The carotid and aortic bodies are the body's oxygen sensors, but the ventilatory response is flat until arterial PO2 drops to roughly 60 mmHg, after which it rises steeply. Option C is wrong in direction: a falling PCO2 removes respiratory drive rather than adding to it, and in any case moment-to-moment carbon dioxide sensing is done by the central chemoreceptors in the medulla, which respond to hydrogen ions generated in CSF.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Regulation of Respiration

question: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) conserves body water mainly by inserting aquaporin water channels into the:
options: C. Thin descending limb of the loop of Henle
explanation: ADH acts on V2 receptors of collecting duct principal cells, moving aquaporin-2 channels into the luminal membrane so water is drawn out into the hypertonic medullary interstitium. The proximal tubule is the tempting choice because it reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtrate, but that reabsorption is obligatory and isosmotic and is not under ADH control, so it cannot be adjusted to concentrate urine.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Urine Concentration and Dilution

question: In a healthy adult, the glomerular filtration rate is approximately:
explanation: GFR averages about 125 mL/min, which works out to roughly 180 litres of filtrate a day, of which more than 99% is reabsorbed. The 500 mL/min option is close to renal plasma flow (about 600-650 mL/min), and confusing filtration rate with plasma flow is the usual error; only about one-fifth of the plasma reaching the glomerulus is actually filtered.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Glomerular Filtration and Renal Blood Flow

question: A patient recovering from a left middle cerebral artery stroke follows every instruction correctly but speaks only in short, effortful, telegraphic phrases. The lesion most likely involves:
options: A. Wernicke's area in the superior temporal gyrus
B. The vermis of the cerebellum
D. Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus
explanation: Broca's area governs motor production of speech, so its damage gives a non-fluent expressive aphasia in which comprehension is preserved and the patient is typically frustrated by his own speech. A Wernicke's lesion is the tempting alternative but produces the opposite picture: speech flows freely yet is meaningless, and comprehension is lost, which does not fit a patient who obeys commands.
citation: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy 8e - The Cerebral Cortex

question: Which set of findings best suggests a cerebellar lesion?
options: A. Resting tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia
B. Intention tremor, past-pointing and a broad-based ataxic gait
C. Spastic weakness with an extensor plantar response
D. Loss of pain and temperature sensation on the opposite side of the body
explanation: The cerebellum coordinates the range, direction and timing of movement, so its damage produces tremor that worsens as the target is approached, dysmetria on finger-nose testing and an unsteady wide-based gait with ipsilateral signs. Option A is the classic trap because it also contains a tremor, but resting tremor with rigidity is extrapyramidal (basal ganglia) disease, and that tremor disappears on voluntary movement.
citation: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy 8e - The Cerebellum and Its Connections

question: Mass sympathetic discharge during acute stress produces:
options: C. Increased peristalsis and gastric secretion
D. Slowing of the heart rate
explanation: Sympathetic activation prepares the body for exertion: beta-2 receptors relax bronchial smooth muscle and alpha-1 receptors contract the radial muscle of the iris to dilate the pupil, while heart rate and contractility rise. Increased peristalsis and gastric secretion is the tempting distractor, but digestion is a parasympathetic (vagal) function that is actively suppressed during sympathetic discharge as blood is diverted to muscle.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - The Autonomic Nervous System and the Adrenal Medulla

question: A patient who has taken oral prednisolone daily for six months stops it abruptly and collapses with hypotension and vomiting. This occurs because prolonged glucocorticoid therapy:
options: B. Suppresses ACTH secretion, causing atrophy of the adrenal cortex
C. Permanently damages the posterior pituitary
D. Increases renal excretion of aldosterone precursors
explanation: Exogenous steroid exerts negative feedback on hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH, and the unstimulated zona fasciculata atrophies, so when the drug is stopped the patient cannot produce cortisol and develops acute adrenal insufficiency; this is why steroids are always tapered. Option A is wrong because the adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines under sympathetic nerve control, not ACTH control, and is unaffected by steroid therapy.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Adrenocortical Hormones

question: Twenty-four hours after a total thyroidectomy, a patient reports tingling around the mouth and develops carpopedal spasm when the blood pressure cuff is inflated. The most likely cause is:
options: B. Injury to or inadvertent removal of the parathyroid glands
D. Hypokalaemia from intraoperative fluid loss
explanation: The parathyroids lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid and are easily bruised or excised, and the resulting fall in parathyroid hormone lowers ionised calcium, producing perioral paraesthesia and the Trousseau sign described here. Thyroid storm is the tempting postoperative complication to name, but it presents with high fever, marked tachycardia, agitation and delirium rather than neuromuscular tetany.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Parathyroid Hormone, Calcitonin and Calcium Metabolism

question: A patient with a mid-shaft fracture of the humerus is unable to extend the wrist and fingers. The nerve most likely injured is the:
explanation: The radial nerve winds around the spiral (radial) groove on the back of the humeral shaft, so a mid-shaft fracture typically produces wrist drop with loss of extension at the wrist, fingers and thumb. Ulnar nerve injury is the common alternative answer, but the ulnar nerve is vulnerable at the medial epicondyle and behind the elbow, and its injury causes clawing and loss of finger abduction rather than wrist drop.
citation: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy 8e - Upper Limb

question: A six-week-old infant is due for the pentavalent vaccine. The correct site for this intramuscular injection is the:
options: C. Anterolateral aspect of the mid-thigh (vastus lateralis)
D. Triceps muscle of the upper arm
explanation: The vastus lateralis in the anterolateral mid-thigh is the recommended intramuscular site in infants because it is the largest muscle mass at this age and has no major nerve or vessel lying over it. The dorsogluteal site is the classic wrong answer: the gluteal muscles remain poorly developed until a child has been walking for some time, and injection there risks sciatic nerve injury and deposition into fat, which reduces vaccine immunogenicity.
citation: MoHFW Universal Immunization Programme - Immunization Handbook for Health Workers

question: Protein digestion begins in the stomach through the action of:
explanation: Chief cells release inactive pepsinogen, which gastric hydrochloric acid converts to pepsin; pepsin works optimally at pH 1.5 to 3.5 and splits proteins into peptides. Trypsin is the tempting choice as a protein-splitting enzyme, but it is pancreatic, is secreted as trypsinogen and is activated by enterokinase only after reaching the duodenum, so it plays no part in gastric digestion.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Digestion and Absorption in the Gastrointestinal Tract

question: A patient with a stone obstructing the common bile duct passes clay-coloured stools and dark urine. The pale stool is explained by:
options: A. Failure of the liver to conjugate bilirubin
B. Bile being unable to reach the intestine, so stercobilin is not formed
C. Increased breakdown of red blood cells
D. Absence of pancreatic lipase in the duodenum
explanation: Stool colour comes from stercobilin, formed when gut bacteria act on conjugated bilirubin delivered in bile; when the duct is blocked no bile reaches the intestine, so the stool is pale while the dammed-back conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and spills into urine, darkening it. Failure of conjugation is the tempting answer, but unconjugated bilirubin is not water-soluble and would give pale urine with normally coloured stool.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Formation and Excretion of Bile

question: A patient with nephrotic syndrome develops generalised oedema. The plasma protein whose loss most directly explains this is:
explanation: Albumin is the smallest and most abundant plasma protein and generates roughly three-quarters of the plasma colloid osmotic pressure of about 25 mmHg that holds fluid inside capillaries; losing it in urine allows filtrate to accumulate in the interstitium. Gamma globulin is also lost in nephrotic syndrome and is the tempting choice, but its deficiency causes susceptibility to infection, and its molecules are too few to contribute meaningfully to oncotic pressure.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Capillary Fluid Exchange and Interstitial Fluid

question: An Rh-negative mother delivers an Rh-positive baby. Anti-D immunoglobulin is given to the mother within 72 hours of delivery in order to:
options: A. Clear fetal Rh-positive cells from her circulation before she forms her own anti-D antibodies
B. Treat anaemia in the newborn
C. Convert the mother's blood group to Rh positive
D. Give her lifelong active immunity against the D antigen
explanation: Fetal red cells that leak into the mother at delivery would otherwise sensitise her, and the resulting maternal IgG anti-D would cross the placenta in a later pregnancy and cause haemolytic disease of the newborn; ready-made anti-D removes those cells before her own immune response starts. Option D is wrong because this is passive immunisation with donated antibody, which is protective for only a few weeks and creates no memory, so the dose must be repeated with every at-risk pregnancy.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Blood Types, Transfusion and Tissue Transplantation

question: In myopia, parallel rays of light entering the relaxed eye are brought to a focus:
options: A. Behind the retina, and the defect is corrected with a convex lens
B. On the retina, and the defect is corrected with a cylindrical lens
C. In front of the retina, and the defect is corrected with a concave lens
D. In front of the retina, and the defect is corrected with a convex lens
explanation: In myopia the eyeball is too long or the refractive power too strong, so rays converge before reaching the retina and distant objects blur; a concave (minus) lens diverges the incoming rays so that the focal point falls back onto the retina. Option D is the trap: it identifies the focal point correctly but prescribes a convex lens, which converges rays further and worsens the error, since convex lenses correct hypermetropia.
citation: AK Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7e - Errors of Refraction

question: The sodium-potassium pump of the cell membrane transports:
options: A. Two sodium ions out for every three potassium ions in
B. Sodium and potassium in the same direction
C. Three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions in, using ATP
D. Potassium out and calcium in
explanation: The Na-K ATPase pumps three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions in with each molecule of ATP, keeping sodium low and potassium high inside the cell and, because more positive charge leaves than enters, contributing directly to the negative resting membrane potential. Option A simply reverses the stoichiometry, which would carry net positive charge inward and make the cell interior less negative rather than more.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Transport of Substances Through Cell Membranes

question: A patient with pneumonia shivers and complains of feeling intensely cold while the recorded temperature is climbing to 39.5 degrees Celsius. The best explanation is that:
options: A. The hypothalamic set point has been raised, so the body generates heat until it reaches the new level
B. The sweat glands have stopped functioning
C. The heat-loss centre has been permanently destroyed by the infection
D. Body temperature has already risen above the set point
explanation: Pyrogens such as interleukin-1 act through prostaglandin E2 to reset the hypothalamic thermostat upward; until the body reaches that higher set point it behaves as though cold, with cutaneous vasoconstriction and shivering, which is why the patient feels chilled even as the thermometer rises. Option D describes the opposite phase, the crisis or defervescence, when the set point falls and the patient flushes and sweats profusely.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e - Body Temperature Regulation and Fever
